lead: The vendor-neutral cloud cert. It proves you can design, deploy, run, secure and fix cloud infrastructure on any provider, and it's the bridge from Security+ to AWS, Azure and CCSP on the Cloud path.

v4.label: V4
v4.note: The current version. CompTIA estimates it retires around 2027, three years after launch. CompTIA recommends 2–3 years as a systems administrator or cloud engineer first.
v4.onote: Summary bullets from CompTIA's V4 page. The full objectives PDF breaks each domain into numbered sub-objectives.

extras.title: Service models
rows: You get VMs, storage and networks. You run the OS and everything above it.
You get a managed runtime. You bring the code and data.
You get a finished app. You manage users and data.
You upload functions that run on events. No servers to manage.

extras.title: Migration strategies
rows: Move it as-is to cloud VMs. Fastest, fewest changes.
Small changes, like moving to a managed database.
Switch to a SaaS product instead.
Retire turns it off; Retain leaves it on-premises for now.

extras.title: Scaling and recovery terms
rows: Give one instance more CPU or RAM. Usually needs a restart.
Add more instances behind a load balancer. Autoscaling does this for you.
How much data you can afford to lose, measured in time.
How fast service must be back.
Point-in-time copy of a disk. Fast, but not a backup if it lives in the same account or region.
A backup nobody can change or delete until it expires. Protects against ransomware.

method: Use the domains above as your checklist. Architecture, Deployment and Security carry over 60% of the exam.
Cloud+ is vendor-neutral, so learn the concept first, then see how AWS and Azure each name it.
Build in a free tier: a VPC with public and private subnets, a VM, a storage bucket, an IAM role. Tear it down when you're done.
Flashcards for service models, migration strategies, scaling terms and RPO/RTO.
Timed practice exams. Review every miss. A common target is 85%+ twice in a row before you book.
tips: They often come first and eat time. Flag them, finish the multiple choice, then come back.
Answers use generic terms (security group, object storage), not one provider's product names.
BEST, FIRST and MOST change the answer. Cost and least privilege are often the tiebreakers.
There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so always pick something.

quiz.q: A web app has a steady baseline load all year, plus heavy spikes every pay week. Which approach gives the LOWEST cost while meeting demand?
o: Reserved capacity for the baseline, plus autoscaled on-demand instances for the spikes
Right. Commit to what you always use (cheapest per hour) and pay on-demand only while the spikes last.
On-demand instances sized for the peak, running all year
You'd pay peak prices every hour of the year, even when most of that capacity sits idle.
Reserved capacity sized for the peak
Reserving peak capacity locks you into paying for idle resources most of the year.
Spot instances for everything
Spot capacity can be taken back with little warning, so it's risky for a baseline that must always be up.

quiz.q: A team needs to run 40 small, isolated microservices that start in seconds and share one host OS kernel. What should they use?
o: Containers
Right. Containers isolate apps while sharing the host kernel, so they're lightweight and start almost instantly.
A VM for each service
VMs each carry a full OS, so 40 of them use far more resources and boot much more slowly.
A Type 2 hypervisor
A Type 2 hypervisor runs VMs on a desktop OS. It doesn't give the lightweight, shared-kernel model.
Bare-metal servers
Dedicated hardware per service is the heaviest, slowest and most expensive option.

quiz.q: A unit must rebuild the same cloud environment in three regions, track every change and roll back bad ones. Which approach BEST fits?
o: Declarative infrastructure as code stored in source control
Right. Templates (like Terraform) build identical environments, and version control gives history and rollback.
A detailed runbook the team follows in the web console
Manual steps drift between regions and leave no reliable record of what actually changed.
Clone the first region's VMs into the others
Cloning copies VMs, not the networks, IAM and settings around them, and gives no change tracking.
Take snapshots before every change
Snapshots help recover a disk; they don't define or rebuild the whole environment.

quiz.q: A legacy app must move to the cloud this month. There's no budget for code changes, and leadership just wants it off the old hardware. Which migration strategy fits?
o: Rehost (lift and shift)
Right. Move it as-is onto cloud VMs: fastest, with no code changes.
Refactor
Refactoring rebuilds the app cloud-native. It takes the most time and code changes.
Replatform
Replatforming makes some changes (like a managed database). The scenario rules out changes.
Repurchase
Repurchasing replaces the app with a SaaS product. That's a different app, not a migration of this one.

quiz.q: A web tier's CPU hits 95% during peak hours, and users get timeouts. The app is stateless and sits behind a load balancer. What is the BEST fix?
o: Horizontal scaling with an autoscaling group
Right. Stateless apps scale out cleanly: add instances when load rises, remove them when it falls.
Vertical scaling to a bigger instance
It helps, but it usually needs a restart and has a ceiling. Scaling out is the cloud-native answer.
Move the app to a different region
Changing regions doesn't add capacity.
Increase the load balancer timeout
Longer timeouts just make users wait longer. The servers are still overloaded.

quiz.q: After a ransomware scare, leadership wants backups that attackers can't delete, even with stolen admin credentials. Which control BEST meets this?
o: Immutable (write-once) backups held in a separate account
Right. Object lock prevents changes until retention ends, and a separate account limits what stolen credentials can reach.
Daily snapshots in the same account
An attacker with admin rights in that account can delete the snapshots too.
Encrypting the backups
Encryption protects confidentiality, not deletion. Attackers can still wipe encrypted backups.
Increasing backup frequency to hourly
More frequent backups improve RPO but are just as deletable.

quiz.q: Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for patching the guest operating system on an IaaS virtual machine?
o: The customer
Right. In IaaS the provider runs the hardware and hypervisor; everything from the guest OS up is yours.
The cloud provider
The provider patches the physical hosts and hypervisor, not your VM's operating system.
Both equally
Responsibilities are split by layer, not shared on the same layer. The guest OS is the customer's.
Whoever deployed the application
Ownership is by service model, not by who deployed the app. In IaaS, that's the customer.

quiz.q: An app on a cloud VM needs to read files from an object storage bucket. What is the MOST secure way to give it access?
o: Attach an IAM role (managed identity) to the VM with read-only access to that bucket
Right. Temporary credentials are issued automatically, nothing is stored on disk, and access is least privilege.
Store an access key in the app's config file
Stored keys can leak through backups, images or source control, and they don't expire on their own.
Make the bucket public
That exposes the files to anyone on the internet.
Give the VM full administrator rights
Far more access than reading one bucket needs. It violates least privilege.

quiz.q: Every time a developer pushes code, a pipeline automatically builds it and runs the test suite before anything is merged. Which practice is this?
o: Continuous integration
Right. CI builds and tests every change as it's committed, catching problems early.
Continuous deployment
Continuous deployment pushes passing changes all the way to production automatically. The scenario stops at build and test.
Infrastructure as code
IaC defines infrastructure in templates. It's not about building and testing app code on each push.
Blue-green deployment
Blue-green is a release technique that switches traffic between two environments.

quiz.q: A developer accidentally pushed cloud access keys to a public code repository an hour ago. What should be done FIRST?
o: Revoke and rotate the exposed keys
Right. Bots scan public repos within minutes. Kill the keys first, then investigate what they were used for.
Delete the commit from the repository
The keys have probably already been copied. Removing them from history doesn't make them invalid.
Review the access logs for misuse
Important, but do it after the keys are revoked, so the attacker can't keep using them while you look.
Make the repository private
The keys were already public for an hour. Hiding them now doesn't stop someone who copied them.

pbqs.title: Who's responsible?
pbqs.scenario: Your unit runs workloads on all three service models. For each task, pick who is responsible in IaaS, PaaS and SaaS: the customer (your unit) or the cloud provider.

rows.req: Physical security of the data center
rows.why: Always the provider. Customers never touch the physical facility.

rows.req: Patching the hypervisor and host hardware
rows.why: The provider owns the virtualization layer in every model.
In IaaS you run the OS. In PaaS and SaaS the provider manages it for you.
In IaaS and PaaS it's your code. In SaaS the provider builds and runs the app.
Always the customer. Even in SaaS, you decide who gets access.
Always the customer. You own your data in every model.

pbqs.title: Diagnose six cloud tickets
pbqs.scenario: Six cloud tickets came in overnight. Read each error and pick the cause. Each answer is used once; two options are distractors.

items.log:
Error: InstanceLimitExceeded
You have requested more vCPU capacity than your current vCPU limit of 32 allows.
items.why: The account hit its vCPU quota. Request a limit increase or right-size the deployment.

items.log:
$ curl -m 5 https://10.0.2.15
curl: (28) Connection timed out
Instance status: running, 2/2 checks passed
Inbound rules: 22/tcp from 10.0.0.0/16
items.why: The instance is healthy, but the security group only allows SSH. HTTPS (443) is never let in.

items.log:
AccessDenied: role/deploy-bot is not authorized to perform
s3:PutObject on resource backups/*
items.why: The role exists but has no permission to write objects to the backup bucket.

items.log:
apt update: could not connect to archive.ubuntu.com
Route table: 10.0.0.0/16 -> local
(no 0.0.0.0/0 route)
items.why: With no default route to a NAT gateway, private instances can't reach the internet for updates.

items.log:
$ dig +short app.unit.example
203.0.113.40
Note: load balancer moved to 198.51.100.7 yesterday
items.why: DNS still points at the old address, so users hit the retired load balancer.

items.log:
Token rejected: issued-at time is in the future
Server clock: 09:42:10
Actual time:  09:47:55
items.why: The server's clock is about six minutes behind, so valid tokens look like they come from the future. Fix NTP.
